newsitem.title: USA: Shuttle Atlantis set to bring U.S. astronaut home.
newsitem.headline: Shuttle Atlantis set to bring U.S. astronaut home.

text.p: Shuttle Atlantis was finally ready to fetch U.S. astronaut Shannon Lucid from the Russian Mir space station, NASA officials said on Sunday.

The $2 billion spaceship, carrying Lucid's replacement and thousands of pounds (kilograms) of cargo, was scheduled to blast off before dawn on Monday on a mission to Mir delayed by nearly seven weeks.
U.S. Air Force meteorologists gave Atlantis a 70 percent chance of good weather for launch during a short seven-minute launch window that opens at 4:54 a.m. EDT (0854 GMT).
Atlantis is due home on Sept. 26, ending Lucid's 188-day mission, a record for a woman and the longest space flight by an American.
Lucid, a 53-year-old biochemist, has been aboard Mir since March and should have come home in early August.
She is the first of six U.S. astronauts who will staff the Russian station into 1998. Her place on Mir will be taken by John Blaha, 54, a former fighter pilot and veteran of four shuttle missions.
The shuttle's launch, originally scheduled for July 31, was postponed by six weeks because NASA ordered the replacement of its twin rocket boosters, fearing a dangerous flaw in the rocket's joints.

Menacing hurricanes lurking off the Florida coast forced NASA to twice haul the shuttle off its launch pad, delaying it a few more days. And a scheduling clash with an unmanned rocket triggered a further delay.
The three-day countdown appeared to be running smoothly on Sunday, ending weeks of difficulty.

"Ever since we picked up the launch count on Friday the 13th, we've had good luck," said Bob Sieck, director of shuttle operations at the Kennedy Space Centre. "The team is as ready to launch as Shannon is ready to come home."
"We're Shannon's prime ticket home," said Paul Dye, the flight director who will orchestrate the mission from NASA's control centre in Houston. "We will be real happy to see her back."
Engineers planned to start loading the shuttle's rust-coloured tank with super cold fuel at about 7:30 p.m. EDT (1130 GMT) on Sunday.
The fiery blast-off will begin a three-day chase through space to catch up with the sprawling Mir complex. The shuttle will link up with Mir late on Wednesday and will remain docked for five days.
Atlantis has a crew of six led by mission commander Bill Readdy. The pilot is Terry Wilcutt and mission specialists are Tom Akers, Jay Apt, Carl Walz and Blaha, who will spend four months aboard Mir.

The shuttle is also carrying about 4,600 pounds (2,070 kgs) of supplies and equipment for Mir and will return to Earth with 2,200 pounds (990 kgs) of scientific samples and other gear from the station.
Without Atlantis, Lucid is effectively stranded in space. NASA has no concrete plans for Lucid's return if the shuttle suffers another major delay or an accident of some kind.

"It's extremely unlikely, but if for some reason we were delayed for months on Atlantis, then we would just have to evaluate the situation and decide at what time and how she needed to come home," said Frank Culbertson, who heads NASA's shuttle-Mir effort.
